Denial cache key concatenates name and folder with '_' and can collide

userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with unescaped '_' separators. Grafana resource UIDs can contain underscores (the tests themselves use UIDs like 'some_dashboard' and 'some_folder_parent'). Dashboard 'a_b' in folder 'c' and dashboard 'a' in folder 'b_c' both produce the key '...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c'. Check consults the denial cache before any permission lookup and returns deny on a hit (service.go lines 116-121), so a denial recorded for one resource causes a false deny for the other for up to the 30s TTL, even when the user has access to it. The key needs an unambiguous encoding (a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash of a structured tuple).

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached denial is checked first and never invalidated, so it can keep blocking a just-created resource

The denial cache is consulted before cached or DB permissions and is only cleared by TTL (30s). The PR's fix for newly created resources is the DB fallback on a permission-cache miss, but that fallback is bypassed whenever the same (user, action, name, folder) was denied within the last 30s. A plausible sequence: a client checks access to a dashboard UID before it exists (authz runs before the storage lookup), gets Allowed=false, and that denial is written at lines 153-155. After the dashboard is created and the creator's permission is written, the creator's check for the same name/folder still returns false until the entry expires. The same staleness applies to any later grant of access. Denials should not short-circuit fresher permission data, or they should be invalidated on create/permission changes.

DB fallback re-reads permissions but still uses the cached folder tree

When the permission cache misses, Check calls getIdentityPermissions and then checkPermission, which reaches checkInheritedPermissions and buildFolderTree (called at line 590). buildFolderTree returns the folderCache entry (TTL 30s) if present (this line). A subfolder created after the tree was cached is absent from that tree, so Ancestors() does not walk through it and grants inherited from its parent folder are not found. Dashboards in the new subfolder are then denied for up to 30s, even though this fallback was added precisely so newly created resources are picked up. The fallback only refreshes the permission map, not the folder data it depends on.

Every denied check missing the permission cache now queries the DB

Before this change, a denied check with a warm permission cache returned without touching the DB, since getUserPermissions read permCache first. Now, when the cached map does not contain the resource, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions (line 139), which runs the full permissionStore.GetUserPermissions query for the action. The 30s denial cache only suppresses repeats for the same (name, folder). Each distinct resource a user is denied on, such as a client probing many UIDs or a user hitting resources they cannot access, therefore produces a full permission query, and sequential checks are not coalesced by singleflight. DB load now scales with the number of distinct denied resources. The fallback should be rate-limited or coalesced per user/action, or the cost should be accepted explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a mapped list without a key

The grafana branch previously passed `key={key}` (the computed rule key). The refactor to `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} ... />` drops the key while the other branches still use it. React will warn about missing keys and fall back to index identity, and component-local state (silence drawer, clone redirect in RuleActionsButtons) is then keyed by position rather than by rule. Pass `key={key}` to restore consistent identity.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence item is shown in the list view but clicking it does nothing

`canSilence` is now true in the list view via the promRule-based ability, so the 'Silence notifications' item renders and calls `handleSilence`. That handler sets `showSilenceDrawer` in RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx, but the drawer is only mounted when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true (see RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx line 104). In the list view `rule` is undefined, so the drawer never renders and the click is a silent no-op. Either migrate SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer to accept the Grafana prom rule, or hide the item when no ruler rule is present.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete (and Pause) disappear from the alert list menu even though permissions allow them

The Delete item is rendered only when `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view no longer passes `rulerRule` (GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with only `promRule`), so the item is never shown, even though `canDelete` now correctly comes from the promRule-based ability. Users with AlertingRuleDelete lose Delete from the list, which the previous GrafanaRuleLoader path offered. The same gating applies to Pause at line 123 (`MenuItemPauseRule rule={rulerRule}` requires a ruler rule), so Pause is also unreachable while `canPause` is true. Either wire delete/pause to the identifier-based path or stop computing these abilities for the list view; as written, the abilities and the rendered menu disagree.

Doc comment still says the loader reads from the Ruler endpoint

The doc comment says 'Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', but after this change the component only queries the Prometheus endpoint (the ruler query was removed). Line 19 in the `expectedRulesCount` prop docs similarly refers to the ruler response, which is no longer consulted. Update the comments to match the implementation.

Every list row now computes both ruler and Grafana ability sets, twice

AlertRuleMenu calls useRulerRuleAbilities (with rulerRule undefined in the list view) and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, and RuleActionsButtons.V2 separately calls useRulerRuleAbility and useGrafanaPromRuleAbility. Each of these runs the full useAll*RuleAbilities computation, including folder lookups and the silence-status query, so each rule row runs the ability logic about four times, even though the ruler-based results are always neutral in the list view. The list page's own comment notes this hook is already called for ~80 rules, so the duplication scales poorly. Compute the abilities once per row or skip the ruler path when rulerRule is absent.

Federated-group check was dropped, so federated rules become editable through useAllAlertRuleAbilities

Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated` from `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. The refactor routes that hook through useAllRulerRuleAbilities(rule.rulerRule, groupIdentifier), which has no access to the group's `source_tenants`, and hard-codes `const isFederated = false` (TODO). useAllAlertRuleAbilities is still exported and used by callers (it is only marked deprecated), so for federated rule groups Update/Delete/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently are now treated as mutable whenever the user has permission. This is a regression of existing behavior for those callers. The federation information should be passed through the new signature rather than removed.

Immutability of list-view rules now depends on a provenance field the Prometheus endpoint must return

`provenance` was added to GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase, and isProvisionedPromRule uses it to disable Update/Delete/Pause for provisioned rules in the list view (previously read from the ruler). If the Prometheus-compatible groups endpoint does not populate `provenance`, provisioned rules will appear editable in the list and editing them will fail server-side. This PR does not include the backend change, so the dependency should be confirmed and called out.

Link to the rule view no longer carries returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component builds `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` without returnTo, so rule-view navigation back to the list (which relies on returnTo, e.g. via useReturnToPrevious) is lost. This is an unmentioned behavior change; restore the returnTo parameter or document its removal.

Test asserts the 4-item list menu, locking in the missing Delete/Pause actions, and does not exercise the actions

The test grants AlertingRuleDelete and expects exactly four menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), so it codifies the omission of Delete (and Pause) in the list view. The comment at line 191 says 'all 4 menu actions should be available' while the user has delete permission, which is misleading. No test verifies that clicking Silence opens the drawer, that Delete is reachable, or that Pause works from the list. The unused `ui.menuItems.delete` helper suggests the delete case was meant to be tested. Tests should reflect the intended list-view action set and cover the click behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range check now runs on the interpolated expression, so $__range queries can be split

querySupportsSplitting() uses isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to stop queries that use $__range from being split. The comment says $__range must reach the backend so it is computed over the split time range. With this PR, runSplitQuery interpolates each query with applyTemplateVariables (line 299) before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting. If request.scopedVars contains __range, the token is already replaced when the check runs, so the check no longer matches. The query is then split, and each chunk is computed over the whole range's value of $__range, so the merged result differs from the unsplit query. The new test only covers $__auto and $step, so nothing catches this. Fix by checking the range variable on the raw expression before interpolation, and update the comment, which becomes misleading.

Empty-expression filter now runs before interpolation, so variables resolving to empty are sent

The filter on query.expr used to run after interpolation, so a target whose expression was a variable resolving to an empty string was dropped. It now runs on the raw expression, before the map that interpolates it. A target such as '$query' whose value is empty is kept, and an empty expression is sent to Loki, which returns a parse error that shows up in the panel. Previously that target was silently skipped. Filter again after interpolation, or keep the previous order.

Shard sub-requests are interpolated a second time, with request.filters applied again

runShardSplitQuery() already calls applyTemplateVariables on every target (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52). Each shard sub-request is then passed to runSplitQuery(), which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the already-interpolated targets, and passes the same request.filters. The updated shard test confirms this: it now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for one target (1 from the shard entry point plus 4 sub-requests). The PR's goal is to interpolate once at the start, but the change repeats the work for every sub-request. Interpolation is not guaranteed idempotent: any value that contains a '$' token after the first pass gets substituted again, and ad-hoc filter handling that appends matchers would run once per sub-request. Fix by interpolating in only one place, for example by having the shard path call an internal runner that skips interpolation.

Test asserts the redundant interpolation count instead of guarding against it

The test now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target. That count encodes the double interpolation of shard sub-requests (one call in runShardSplitQuery plus one per runSplitQuery sub-request), so the test locks in the behavior the PR should avoid. No test checks that each target is interpolated exactly once, and none checks that request.filters is applied once. Those assertions are needed once the double interpolation is fixed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID dropped from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line

The old logRequest appended a traceID field (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)) to the completed-request log. That block is removed and the new log call m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) does not add a traceID. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware's instrumentContext also does not add traceID (it only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname). Plugin request logs therefore lose trace correlation, which is a user-visible regression for debugging. The traceID should be carried into the contextual attributes or appended here again.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so recorded calls are lost

FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a new instance whose InfoLogs/WarnLogs/etc. are not connected to the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now writes 'Plugin Request Completed' via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a test that injects a TestLogger and then inspects its InfoLogs will see nothing. Such assertions would fail or pass vacuously after this change. The fake should return the receiver (or share its recording state) so the contextual calls are observable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests and the moved logging behaviour is untested

This PR moves the plugin context attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of LoggerMiddleware and into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and changes LoggerMiddleware to log via FromContext. No test covers that the contextual attributes are attached for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics, or that LoggerMiddleware's completed-request log picks them up. The only test touched is the renamed metrics test, which checks only metrics. A regression in the attribute set would go unnoticed.

PR description says the contextual logger moved into LoggerMiddleware, but it is a separate middleware

The PR description says the contextual logger was moved 'to the LoggerMiddleware'. In the code, the contextual logger is a new, separate ContextualLoggerMiddleware (this file), which is wired as its own entry in CreateMiddlewares. Anyone relying on the description when reviewing or reverting this change will be misled about where the behaviour lives.

Stale test name after the rename

The file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the type is now MetricsMiddleware, but the test is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. The rename is incomplete and the test name now refers to a type that no longer exists.

Undocumented ordering dependency: request log fields now depend on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running earlier

LoggerMiddleware no longer adds pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID or uname itself. It relies on the contextual logger already being in the ctx, which requires ContextualLoggerMiddleware to be placed before LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares. If someone reorders the stack or omits the contextual middleware, the completed-request log silently loses these fields with no error. The removed MetricsMiddleware comment ('this middleware should live at the top of the middleware stack') is not restated for the new middleware, and neither NewContextualLoggerMiddleware nor NewLoggerMiddleware documents the requirement.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with the insert

CountDevices and the following INSERT are separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first-time requests from distinct devices can each see count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the number of devices can exceed the configured limit by up to the number of concurrent first requests. The limit is therefore soft. If it is meant to be strict (for example for licensing), the check and insert need to be a single conditional statement or a transaction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice comment and error description do not match behavior

The comment says the function updates a device 'that has been updated between the given times', but it takes no time arguments. The window is hard-coded relative to device.UpdatedAt (30 days back to 1 minute ahead). The function also returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever no row matches, which includes devices that simply expired or were deleted concurrently. The comment and the error meaning should be corrected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected device is cached as tagged, so later requests bypass the limit

tagDeviceUI sets the device key in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and never removes it when that call fails. When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the first request is rejected, but the key stays cached for about 29 minutes. Every later request from that device ID hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. The device is never counted, so after one rejection it keeps anonymous access for the rest of the cache window. The fix is to cache the key only after a successful tag, or to delete it on error. No test covers a second request after a rejection.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Constructor signature changed for a DI-wired provider without any wire changes

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore now requires a deviceLimit argument. These are Wire providers, but no wire.go or wire_gen.go file is in the change set. If the generated injector still passes an AnonStore into this constructor, the build breaks. In either case the service now constructs its own store, so the AnonStore can no longer be injected or replaced in tests. The generated wiring needs to be checked and regenerated.

Device limit tests miss the update path and the request-level behavior

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the store level with limit 1. It does not cover an already-known device still being updated once the limit is reached (the updateDevice path). It also does not test TagDevice or Authenticate, where the rejected-device caching bug at impl.go:87 lives, so a retry after rejection is never checked. There is no test for a limit above 1 either.

Device tagging moved onto the synchronous login path using the request context

Previously tagging ran in a goroutine with a detached 2-minute context and panic recovery. Now Authenticate waits for TagDevice on the request context. For every device not in the cache, login blocks on a DB write and, when a limit is configured, on a COUNT over the 30-day window (CreateOrUpdateDevice). If the client disconnects, the request context is cancelled and the write may fail with context canceled. The device key has already been cached at impl.go:87, so the device stays untagged for about 29 minutes. Only the limit check needs to be synchronous. The tagging write should not depend on the request context, or the cache entry should be cleared on failure.

New device_limit option is not documented

The [auth.anonymous] device_limit key is parsed here, but it is not added to conf/defaults.ini or the configuration docs, and the PR's docs checkbox is unchecked. Operators cannot discover the option or its semantics: 0 means unlimited, the count covers devices updated in the last 30 days, and negative values are treated as unlimited.

Requests without a device ID or a parseable IP skip the limit entirely

TagDevice returns nil before any limit check when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is empty (line 121), and also when the remote address cannot be parsed (line 128). Authenticate then proceeds and grants anonymous access. The device ID is fully client-supplied, so a client that omits the header is never counted or rejected, and the limit cannot be enforced for those requests once it is reached. Anonymous requests that are not tagged should be checked against the limit, or rejected when the limit is reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine batch progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists

The informational logs added in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags use r.log.Error for every batch, including successful ones (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579). Every cleanup batch therefore emits error-level entries even when nothing failed. The 'Annotations to clean by time/count' and 'Tags to clean' entries also include the whole `ids` slice, up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs per line. With a large backlog this floods the error log with thousands of IDs and hides real errors. The `err` field logged at these points is always nil, because errors already return earlier. These should be Debug-level messages without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to the PR

The change from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1` alters how often every background cleanup job runs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations), not just annotation cleanup. The PR description does not mention it, and it looks like a leftover debugging change. It raises the periodic DB load of all cleanup jobs roughly tenfold, and the annotation job can run for up to the 9-minute clean timeout. Revert it unless the new interval is an intentional, separately reviewed change.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-SQLite delete now binds one parameter per ID, which breaks for large batch sizes

The non-SQLite branch builds one `?` placeholder and one bind argument per ID. The previous DELETE only inlined LIMIT, so the statement did not depend on the batch size. MySQL prepared statements and the Postgres wire protocol reject more than 65535 bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is an unbounded int64 config value, so a batch size above that limit would make every cleanup batch fail on MySQL/Postgres, where it previously worked. Validate or cap the batch size, or chunk the DELETE IN list to a bounded number of parameters.

Quadratic string concatenation when building the inline SQLite ID list

`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration. For a batch of up to 32767 IDs, which is the case the new test exercises, this copies on the order of several GB of bytes and performs tens of thousands of allocations on every cleanup iteration. Build the list once with strings.Builder, strconv.AppendInt, or strings.Join over strconv.FormatInt.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches the bare logger to the context, dropping name/kind/method fields

Line 96 builds a 'log' with name, kind and method values, but line 97 stores d.Log in the context instead. Storage implementations that log via klog.FromContext therefore lose the per-request fields that the other methods (Create, Get, Update) propagate.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records the legacy duration as a storage duration

The goroutine at line 166 calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). The legacy latency and error are attributed to the storage metric, which corrupts the storage/legacy comparison this dual-writer is meant to produce. It should be recordLegacyDuration.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete passes the object name where the kind label is expected in the storage duration metric

The call is d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument is the kind/resource label used by the other calls (options.Kind). Passing the object name produces wrong metric labels and creates one time series per deleted object, which is an unbounded cardinality explosion in Prometheus.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

The goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause. Create returns immediately after the storage write, and net/http cancels the request context when ServeHTTP returns. The legacy Create therefore usually runs with an already-cancelled context, and SQL-backed legacy stores abort the write. The resulting error is only recorded in a metric, so the legacy copy silently diverges. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The fix is to detach the context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before adding the 10s timeout.

Each write spawns an unbounded goroutine with a 10s timeout and no backpressure

Every successful write starts a goroutine that holds the object and context for up to 10 seconds. If the legacy store is slow, goroutines and held objects accumulate proportionally to write rate with no concurrency cap or queue. This can increase memory usage and goroutine count under write load.

Errors from async legacy writes are discarded without logging

In the Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection goroutines the legacy error is only passed to a duration metric as a boolean (e.g. line 56 errObjectSt != nil). The error value and the object identity are never logged. The previous synchronous code logged these failures. Operators have no way to find which objects failed to reach legacy storage, which matters because this is the only signal that the 'safe measure' copy is missing data.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order relative to later writes

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object ordering. A Create followed quickly by a Delete of the same name can run the legacy Delete before the legacy Create. The Delete then hits NotFound (ignored), and the Create lands, leaving a legacy copy of an object that unified storage has already deleted. Update/Delete races can similarly leave resurrected or stale legacy objects. Nothing reconciles these because the error is not surfaced.

Legacy Update recomputes the update from the same objInfo, so legacy can persist a different object than unified

The previous implementation computed the updated object once and handed the same result to both stores. This version passes the raw objInfo to d.Storage.Update and then, in a goroutine, to d.Legacy.Update. The legacy call invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject a second time, against the legacy store's current object, and after the handler may have returned. A patch-style or stateful UpdatedObjectInfo can then yield a different result than the one written to unified storage, so the two stores diverge with no error surfaced.

Method comments describe synchronous dual writes that are no longer synchronous

The comment on Create says it writes to LegacyStorage and Storage, and the DeleteCollection comment says it deletes from both. The legacy write is now asynchronous and its failures are not reported to the caller. The comments should say so, otherwise readers will assume legacy consistency guarantees that do not exist.

Mode 3 tests share one mock between storage and legacy, so they cannot verify which backend was called

The tests use one mock.Mock for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so an expectation set for one backend also matches calls to the other. The Create error case sets up no storage expectation, yet passes because the legacy expectation for failingObj matches the storage call. Async legacy calls are never awaited or asserted, and there is no AssertExpectations or AssertNotCalled check. The tests therefore do not verify the core Mode 3 contract: reads hit only storage, and writes go to storage first and then to legacy.

New mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy state immediately after writes that go to legacy asynchronously

The new 'file, mode 3' and 'unified storage, mode 3' subtests run doPlaylistTests. That helper checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoint right after k8s creates and checks legacy GETs right after k8s PUT/PATCH (for example the list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a goroutine after the response, so these assertions race with it and the subtests will be flaky. The helper needs to poll or wait for legacy convergence in mode 3.

Storage failures are recorded as legacy failures (Create and Update)

In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the error branch for the storage write calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). Failures of the unified storage write are therefore counted against legacy, which misattributes errors and sends operators to the wrong backend. These should be recordStorageDuration calls.

Test name says 'not implemented' but the case tests a storage error

The case named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented' now exercises a normal List path where the storage mock returns an error. The name is a leftover from the old stub and misdescribes the behavior under test.

Unified NotFound now skips the legacy delete, which the previous code deliberately did not do

The removed code tolerated IsNotFound from the storage Delete and still deleted from legacy. This version returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so a NotFound from unified never reaches legacy. An object that exists only in legacy stays there forever. A later Create succeeds in unified, and its async legacy Create fails with AlreadyExists, silently. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR and needs an explicit decision and a test.

Unrelated go.work.sum churn, including a duplicated checksum line

The go.work.sum changes add checksum entries for grafana-azure-sdk-go, grafana-plugin-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters/sdk and others that have nothing to do with the dual-writer feature. The grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery go.mod line at 408 duplicates the unchanged line just above it. These changes look like a stale workspace file and should be dropped from this PR.

Untracked goroutines have no panic recovery and Destroy does not wait for them

The legacy goroutines have no recover(). A panic in a legacy implementation inside a goroutine terminates the whole process, whereas the previous synchronous calls ran in the request handler where net/http recovers the panic. Destroy() (lines 172-175) also tears down d.Legacy while these goroutines may still be using it, and there is no WaitGroup or other tracking to drain in-flight writes at shutdown.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-checked read after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent cold-start callers each reload the manifest

The RLock check at lines 41-47 happens once, and the write lock is taken at line 48 without re-checking the cache. If several goroutines miss the cache at the same time, they each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read the manifest file (and possibly the CDN) even though the first one has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache`. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `Lock()` would avoid the redundant work in non-dev mode.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race fix has no regression test

The PR fixes a data race on the package-level `entryPointAssetsCache`, but no test is added or changed. A test that calls `GetWebAssets` concurrently from multiple goroutines (in both dev and non-dev environments, run under `go test -race`) would confirm the fix and keep the race from coming back. Without it, nothing in CI exercises the locking path.

Dev mode now serializes every request behind a write lock held across file and network I/O

In dev mode the condition `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil` is always false, so every call falls through to `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and holds the exclusive lock for the whole reload. That reload can call `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an HTTP request made with `http.DefaultClient`, which has no timeout) and then read and parse the manifest from disk. Before this change, concurrent dev-mode requests ran in parallel. Now they queue behind one another, and a slow CDN response stalls every caller, including ones that only need the read path. Waiting callers also ignore their own `ctx` cancellation while blocked on the lock. Consider doing the reload outside the lock, or only holding the lock while publishing the result.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the feature flag check is dead logic

The helper reads FlagSqlExpressions, then returns false on both branches of `if enabled`. The flag value has no effect, so the SQL case always returns 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. The name suggests flag-driven enablement, which misleads anyone who later wants to re-enable SQL expressions by flag. They would have to rewrite the helper, and the flag lookup is still evaluated on the SQL path, which the previous code did not do. If h.features is ever nil, this now panics for SQL queries where it previously did not. Replace the helper with an unconditional rejection, or keep the flag check and drop the forced false.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL expression parsing and execution tests will fail, and no test covers the new rejection

TablesList now always fails because DB.RunCommands in db.go always returns an error, so NewSQLCommand also always fails. Any existing test expecting TablesList or NewSQLCommand to return table names, or expecting SQL command execution to produce frames, will now fail. The PR does not touch any test files. Nothing in the diff asserts that a SQL query is rejected at ReadQuery (reader.go, SQL case), or that the stub DB returns errors. Either the affected tests are left broken, or the PR is missing coverage for the new behavior. Update or remove the old SQL tests and add a test for the rejection path.

false_positives.candidate:
Nil pointer dereference when building the unloading threshold fails (pre-existing)

This is not introduced by the PR, but it is in the same file. `unloading, err := NewThresholdCommand(...)` is followed by `unloading.Invert = true` before the `if err != nil` check on the next line. If NewThresholdCommand returns a nil pointer on error, a user-supplied invalid unloadCondition evaluator type causes a panic while parsing the query. Move the error check above the field assignment.

UnmarshalSQLCommand bypasses the ExpressionQueryReader gate

The new check lives only in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery. UnmarshalSQLCommand is exported and calls NewSQLCommand directly with no feature or enable check. Right now SQL execution is blocked only because the stub DB returns errors. If a real engine is reintroduced in pkg/expr/sql/db.go, this path would reach it without the gate. Put the guard in NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand too, so the protection does not depend on a single call path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the build lock lets duplicate builds for the same key run concurrently

Removing cacheMu from BuildIndex means concurrent builds for the same NamespacedResource now run in parallel, and nothing dedupes them (the TODO in getOrCreateIndex notes this gap). Two concurrent Search requests on a new namespace each run a full build, roughly doubling CPU and memory for that namespace. For file indexes, the second caller gets bleve's path-exists error from bleve.New at this line while the first build is still in flight. The old lock did not dedupe either, but it serialized the work. The speedup holds only for distinct keys, so the PR should add per-key deduplication or state this limitation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. The PR adds a TotalDocs call to searchSupport.init (search.go line 216) that runs right after the watch goroutine starts, and that goroutine can call BuildIndex for a namespace with no index yet. A concurrent map iteration and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error in Go, so this can crash the process. Take cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex span context is discarded, so the span has no children

BuildIndex starts its span with '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and never passes the derived context to bleve.New, the builder, or the flush. The span therefore has no children, which is inconsistent with the trace-propagation fix this PR describes in search.go's build and init. Use 'ctx, span :=' and pass ctx onward.

Constructor error path does not release context or lifecycle resources

When Init fails, NewResourceServer logs and returns without calling s.cancel() or stopping the lifecycle. The background context and any resources opened by lifecycle.Init (for the sql backend, the DB handle from dbProvider.Init) are never released. Now that construction performs real I/O, the error path should clean up, for example by calling s.cancel() and stopping the lifecycle when Init fails.

Constructor now performs DB init and full index build synchronously with no deadline

NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle.Init (for the sql backend: DB provider init and ping) and the full search index build via search.init, then returns any failure as a constructor error. The context is a background context with no deadline, so a slow or unreachable database, or a long index build, now blocks construction indefinitely instead of failing individual RPCs. Any dependency-injection graph that constructs ResourceServer now runs this I/O at construction time, before service Init phases, and fails startup on any init error. The PR does not show that every caller constructs it after the database is ready. Add a startup timeout and confirm construction order for all callers.

Lazy-to-eager init change ships with no tests

The change removes the Init guard from about ten handlers, reorders initialization (search init now runs before initWatcher), and makes NewResourceServer fail on init errors. No unit tests are added or updated; the only test touched adds a postgres skip. Nothing verifies that the constructor returns the init error, that the broadcaster is ready for Watch immediately after construction, or that mocked backends in existing server tests tolerate the eager GetResourceStats, WatchWriteEvents and lifecycle calls now made during construction.

Missing indexes are still built under the gRPC request context

The PR's goal is to stop index builds from being cancelled by request contexts, but Search still builds any index missing from the cache with the request context: Search calls getOrCreateIndex(ctx), which calls s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0), which calls BuildIndex(ctx) and ListIterator(ctx). Namespaces skipped at startup (count at or below InitMinCount) and namespaces created after startup still take this path, so a client disconnect or deadline mid-build still aborts the build. The hard-coded size of 10 is also far below any realistic FileThreshold, so these indexes are always memory-only even when large. Build missing indexes with a server-lifetime context, or document that this path remains request-scoped.

Poller span is never ended on the listLatestRVs error path

In poller, the span started at line 580 is ended only at the bottom of the tick. The error branch at lines 583-586 logs, resets the ticker, and executes 'continue' without calling span.End(), so the span is never ended and is never exported on every failed tick. Call span.End() before continue, or end the span in each branch.

Post-Stop rejection of RPCs was lost when the Init guards were removed

Previously every RPC called s.Init, which returned s.initErr, and Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', so RPCs after Stop were rejected. With the Init guards removed from Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob and GetBlob, nothing reads initErr after construction. This assignment is now dead, and requests arriving after Stop are served against a stopped service: writes still reach the database and watch streams run on a cancelled context. Keep a post-stop check in the handlers or document the new behavior.

Postgres skip removes the only storage-server startup test for postgres runs

This skip disables TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer for every postgres run. That test exercises the storage-server startup path that this PR moves into the NewResourceServer constructor, so the PR now has no coverage of that path on postgres. The skip is unrelated to the PR description, has no tracking issue, and removes coverage rather than fixing the test. Link an issue or keep the test running.

Shared err variable written from concurrent index builds can swallow errors

In init, the errgroup closure writes the outer err (declared at line 181) and increments totalBatchesIndexed (line 189) from up to initWorkers goroutines at once. The closure returns that shared variable, so a failing build can be overwritten by another goroutine's successful s.build (which sets err to nil) before the closure's return value is read. group.Wait() then reports nil and startup continues with a namespace's index missing. The race detector also flags this. Because init now runs synchronously inside NewResourceServer, a swallowed error means the server starts with incomplete search results. Use a closure-local err and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

Watch consumer does not check channel close and panics on nil event during shutdown

The goroutine consuming the watch channel does 'v := <-events' without checking the ok flag. The sql backend's poller closes its stream when the backend is stopped (deferred close after <-b.done), so after Stop every receive yields nil. handleEvent then dereferences evt.Type on its first line and panics in a background goroutine, which takes down the process during graceful shutdown. The context used here is context.Background() and is never cancelled, so nothing stops the loop. This predates the PR, but it is the init path the PR changes and now runs at construction. Check ok and return when the channel closes.

WriteEvent discards the span context, so the PR's trace fix is incomplete

The PR claims to fix trace propagation, but only GetResourceStats was changed to use the derived context. WriteEvent still does '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and then passes the original ctx to create/update/delete, so those spans become siblings of the WriteEvent span rather than children. The same pattern remains in ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388). Either fix all of them or stop describing the trace propagation as fixed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup removes an IDP named literally 'alias' instead of the IDPs created in the loop

The cleanup registers testRealm().identityProviders().get('alias')::remove, which targets a nonexistent provider with the literal alias 'alias', so the 'idp-alias-N' providers created in the loop are never removed (the same mistake is repeated at line 425 for 'idp-alias-20'). The leftover IDPs stay linked to the organization and can leak into other tests in the class or leave the cleanup itself failing with a 404. The cleanup should capture the actual alias in a final local and call get(thatAlias)::remove.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache search key maps null and empty organizationId to the same entry, although the underlying queries differ

searchKey is computed as organizationId != null ? organizationId : "". The default getForLogin only adds the ORGANIZATION_ID criterion when organizationId is non-null, so a null argument (all organizations) and an empty-string argument (criterion applied with an empty value) are different queries. Both are cached under the same cacheKey and searchKey, so a call with one value can return the cached result of the other, depending on call order. No current caller passes an empty string, so the impact is latent, but the key construction is ambiguous. Use a distinct sentinel for the null case.

getForLogin Javadoc omits the new requirement that org-linked IDPs must be public

The Javadoc says an IDP can be used for login if it is enabled, not link-only, and not hidden on login. The PR adds to getLoginPredicate a rule that IDPs bound to an organization must have BROKER_PUBLIC=true, and the ORG_ONLY query filters on the same flag. Neither this Javadoc nor the LoginFilter enum documentation mentions it, so SPI implementers and callers reading the contract will not know that org-bound IDPs need the public flag to be listed for login.

testCacheIDPForLogin never checks that creating or removing a login-eligible IDP invalidates the login caches

Step 1 only creates a hidden IDP and removes a disabled IDP, and asserts that the caches survive. Neither operation qualifies for login, so the registerIDPLoginInvalidation calls in create() and remove() are never shown to invalidate anything. A regression that drops those calls would pass this test. The test also has no scenario where the owning organization is disabled, which is the case where the wrapper changes login eligibility and where update() currently skips invalidation incorrectly. Add steps that create and remove a login-eligible IDP, and one that changes a linked IDP's login status while its org is disabled.

update() judges the 'before' state with the org-aware wrapper, so login-cache invalidation is skipped for IDPs of disabled orgs

update() gets idpById via getById(), which returns the organization-aware wrapper from createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the owning organization is disabled. So when the org is disabled, getLoginPredicate().test(original) is false even though the IDP is raw-enabled and its id is in the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL login lists (the DB query does not check org enablement). If the update then also makes the IDP non-login (hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly, BROKER_PUBLIC=false, or enabled=false), both predicates are false and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate returns without invalidating. When the org is later re-enabled, getForLogin returns the stale entry; the wrapper now reports enabled, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), so a hidden or link-only IDP is shown on the login page. remove() avoids this by using the raw idpDelegate.getByAlias(), so the 'original' state should likewise come from the raw model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById) rather than the wrapped getById().

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle

The method returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is typically the SUN provider for PKCS12/JKS. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle provider. Any caller that uses it to register or look up the BC provider silently gets the wrong provider. The other unimplemented methods in this class throw UnsupportedOperationException, so this is also inconsistent with the class's own pattern. It should throw UnsupportedOperationException, or return the real BC provider if one is available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation

order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Any CryptoProvider implementation not updated in this PR, including out-of-tree providers and any in-repo test or helper implementations not shown in the diff, will fail to compile. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep the SPI source-compatible while still letting providers override the priority.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Code appears adapted from Bouncy Castle without attribution

The readTagNumber/readLength logic and comments, such as the quotation of X.690 8.1.2.4.2 and the 'Note: -1 will pass' comment, look taken from Bouncy Castle's ASN1InputStream. ASN1Encoder.writeLength looks similarly derived from DEROutputStream. Bouncy Castle is MIT-licensed. If this code is adapted, the source's license notice and attribution must be kept. The file header only names Red Hat copyright and @author rmartinc, which does not reflect the provenance. The author should confirm provenance and add attribution.

ECDSA test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks a round-trip

The key pair is always generated with the default EC size (P-256), including for the ES384 and ES512 cases. For ES512 the coordinates are then only 32 bytes, so the 66-byte coordinate path in integerToBytes is only exercised with padding and never with real P-521 values. The test also only asserts that RS -> DER -> RS is the identity. It never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by java.security.Signature.verify, and never checks an independently produced DER signature. A bug where both directions are wrong in a consistent way would still pass. The test should generate a curve matching each algorithm (P-256/P-384/P-521) and verify the reconstructed DER signature with the JDK verifier.

Equal-order crypto providers are now resolved silently by classpath order, including FIPS vs default

detectProvider now sorts by order() descending and takes the first entry. The old guard that threw 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' was removed, but no tie-breaking rule was added. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() == 200. If two of them are on the classpath, the winner is whichever ServiceLoader lists first, with no error or warning. In a FIPS deployment where the non-FIPS default provider jar is also present, this can silently select the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider. The javadoc for order() in CryptoProvider does not say what happens on ties. Also, every discovered provider is instantiated before selection. FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE into the global java.security provider list and modifies security properties, so those side effects happen even when the provider is not selected. Previously this configuration failed fast.

Every AuthzClient.create() now requires CryptoProvider SPI discovery to succeed

create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) unconditionally. Before this change, a plain token or HTTP client needed no crypto provider. Now, if ServiceLoader finds no CryptoProvider, init throws IllegalStateException and client construction fails even for non-ECDSA use. This can happen when the authz-client jar's META-INF/services entry is dropped by a shade or fat-jar build, or when the classloader does not expose it. Initialization is also process-wide and first-wins, so the first AuthzClient created fixes the JVM-wide provider for every other library. Consider initializing lazily only on the ECDSA signing path, or handling discovery failure.

No test covers the new provider selection (order precedence and ties)

The change replaces a fail-fast policy with order-based selection and tie behavior, but no test exercises detectProvider with multiple providers, different orders, or equal orders. A unit test for precedence and tie handling would catch regressions such as the FIPS/default tie described above.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal cleanup is gated on the V1 feature flag, disabling it entirely for V2-only deployments

The whole listener is now wrapped in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), the V1 flag. The base code had no guard, so under V2-only the role, group and client removal handlers ran through management(), which selects V2. With this change they never run when only V2 is enabled. Permission state for deleted roles, groups and clients is then left behind. The guard appears to be a workaround for the exception in the ClientRemovedEvent branch, not a fix. The guard should check the feature actually in use, and the V2 client cleanup should be implemented or explicitly made a no-op.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null dereference when the 'Clients' type resource does not exist

getResourceTypeResource(...) returns null when the 'Clients' resource type resource is absent from the store, or when the schema does not apply. That null is passed straight to getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a check. The absence is realistic for realms whose admin permissions were initialized before this change, because init() never adds the Clients resource (see AdminPermissionsSchema.java:226). Any per-client permission check for a client without its own resource then fails with an NPE instead of returning false.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead getEvaluationContext method and unused imports copied from V1

getEvaluationContext is private and never called, since canExchangeTo throws. Its supporting imports (ClientModelIdentity, DefaultEvaluationContext, EvaluationContext) exist only for it. The logger field (line 51), the TOKEN_EXCHANGE static import (line 46) and the Scope import (line 27) are also unused. This is leftover copy-paste that will confuse maintainers about what V2 actually supports.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

false_positives.candidate:
All-clients grants are ignored for any client that has its own resource

hasPermission(client, scope) only consults the 'Clients' type resource when no per-client resource exists. If a per-client permission exists for client A (for example CONFIGURE), then canManage(A), canConfigure(A), canMapRoles(A), canMapCompositeRoles(A) and canMapClientScopeRoles(A) evaluate only A's resource. An all-clients MANAGE or MAP_ROLES grant is therefore silently ignored for A but honored for every other client. This contradicts the Javadoc added in ClientPermissionEvaluator ('For V2 only: Also if the caller has a permission to ... all clients'). It is also inconsistent with canView(client), which checks the all-clients VIEW grant unconditionally via canView(). No test combines a per-client permission with an all-clients permission for clients, so this is not covered.

Authorization queries throw UnsupportedOperationException instead of returning a decision

canExchangeTo is an authorization decision, yet it throws. The same is true of isPermissionsEnabled (line 188), getPermissions (line 203) and the mapRoles/manage/configure/view Policy factories. MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now returns this class, so callers that previously received the inherited V1 behaviour now get a server error on these paths. The PR does not show that these callers are unreachable under V2. Returning false, or implementing the method, would be safer than a 500.

Client deletion fails under V2 because the removal listener calls an unimplemented V2 method

The ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, and this PR makes clients() return ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled (ClientPermissionsV2.java:193) throws UnsupportedOperationException. The exception propagates out of event publishing, so deleting any client fails when the V1 flag is also enabled. The V1 flag gate on the listener (line 77) hides this for V2-only deployments instead of fixing it. No test in the PR deletes a client under V2, so the regression is not caught.

No upgrade path for realms already initialized before the Clients type and scopes existed

init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, so realms initialized before this change never receive the new Clients resource type or the new scopes configure, map-roles-client-scope and map-roles-composite. Creating a client permission in such a realm then fails in getOrCreateResource (line 108) with ModelException 'No scopes found.', and read paths hit the null type resource in ClientPermissionsV2 line 219. The PR needs a sync step for missing resource types and scopes, or it must explain why existing realms are unsupported.

getResourceName has no mapping for Clients resources

For the USERS type, getResourceName maps the internal id to a readable username. For the CLIENTS type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is not derived from the client. Resources for clients are named with the client's internal UUID, so the result will not identify the client by clientId. The USERS branch shows the intended behaviour and the CLIENTS case is missing.

requireView() Javadoc describes a boolean return for a void method

The Javadoc for requireView() says 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and should throw ForbiddenException when canView() is false. The same mistake appears in the Javadoc for requireViewClientScopes() (line 101). Both were added in this PR and should describe the throw behaviour, as the requireX methods above them do.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Feature gate for the 'check' subcommand is untested

The new feature gate was added to both UpdateCompatibilityMetadata and UpdateCompatibilityCheck, but testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the 'metadata' subcommand. The 'check' gate, which returns FEATURE_DISABLED before reading the file, has no test. Its early return is the only path that skips validateConfig and file reading for check, so a regression there would go unnoticed.

Feature-disabled and recreate exit codes are never asserted

The PR changes the exit-code contract that the docs tell automation to rely on: RECREATE becomes 3 and FEATURE_DISABLED becomes 4. testFeatureNotEnabled only calls assertError on the message and never checks the exit code, so a regression to 0 or 1 would pass. Likewise testWrongVersions (lines 97 and 106) asserts only error text and never checks that the recreate result exits with 3. No test covers the recreate exit code at all, even though the docs present it as the signal for CI/CD pipelines.

Null-strategy test path runs without rolling-updates, contradicting the docs

createInitialDeployment returns early when updateStrategy is null, so the rolling-updates feature is only enabled for non-null strategies. The docs added in advanced-configuration.adoc say the feature 'must be enabled. Otherwise, the Operator will fail.' Either that doc statement is overstated (the operator only fails when update settings are present), or the null-strategy variants of testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount run in a configuration the docs say is invalid. The PR should make the doc precise or enable the feature for the null case too.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian account TOTP step text replaced with Italian

The `totpStep1` value is replaced with an Italian sentence ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:"). Lithuanian users will see Italian text on the account TOTP setup page. The value should be a Lithuanian translation of the English source ("Install one of the following applications on your mobile:"). The same copy-paste error appears in the login messages_lt.properties file.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Traditional Chinese text in the Simplified Chinese bundle

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order crypto providers are now resolved silently by classpath order, including FIPS vs default

detectProvider now sorts by order() descending and takes the first entry. The old guard that threw 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' was removed, but no tie-breaking rule was added. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() == 200. If two of them are on the classpath, the winner is whichever ServiceLoader lists first, with no error or warning. In a FIPS deployment where the non-FIPS default provider jar is also present, this can silently select the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider. The javadoc for order() in CryptoProvider does not say what happens on ties. Also, every discovered provider is instantiated before selection. FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE into the global java.security provider list and modifies security properties, so those side effects happen even when the provider is not selected. Previously this configuration failed fast.

Every AuthzClient.create() now requires CryptoProvider SPI discovery to succeed

create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) unconditionally. Before this change, a plain token or HTTP client needed no crypto provider. Now, if ServiceLoader finds no CryptoProvider, init throws IllegalStateException and client construction fails even for non-ECDSA use. This can happen when the authz-client jar's META-INF/services entry is dropped by a shade or fat-jar build, or when the classloader does not expose it. Initialization is also process-wide and first-wins, so the first AuthzClient created fixes the JVM-wide provider for every other library. Consider initializing lazily only on the ECDSA signing path, or handling discovery failure.

ECDSA test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks a round-trip

The key pair is always generated with the default EC size (P-256), including for the ES384 and ES512 cases. For ES512 the coordinates are then only 32 bytes, so the 66-byte coordinate path in integerToBytes is only exercised with padding and never with real P-521 values. The test also only asserts that RS -> DER -> RS is the identity. It never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by java.security.Signature.verify, and never checks an independently produced DER signature. A bug where both directions are wrong in a consistent way would still pass. The test should generate a curve matching each algorithm (P-256/P-384/P-521) and verify the reconstructed DER signature with the JDK verifier.

Code appears adapted from Bouncy Castle without attribution

The readTagNumber/readLength logic and comments, such as the quotation of X.690 8.1.2.4.2 and the 'Note: -1 will pass' comment, look taken from Bouncy Castle's ASN1InputStream. ASN1Encoder.writeLength looks similarly derived from DEROutputStream. Bouncy Castle is MIT-licensed. If this code is adapted, the source's license notice and attribution must be kept. The file header only names Red Hat copyright and @author rmartinc, which does not reflect the provenance. The author should confirm provenance and add attribution.

The change replaces a fail-fast policy with order-based selection and tie behavior, but no test exercises detectProvider with multiple providers, different orders, or equal orders. A unit test for precedence and tie handling would catch regressions such as the FIPS/default tie described above.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime key and raises TypeError

The endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime" and the value is a datetime object, which math.floor rejects with TypeError. build_cursor calls key(results[0]) whenever the first page has results, so every request with optimized_pagination=true from an admin that returns at least one audit log row fails with a 500. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class also lacks the strftime-to-milliseconds conversion, and value_from_cursor returns the raw integer, so cursors could not be used for datetime comparisons even if the TypeError were avoided. Base paginator silently clamps negative next-cursor offsets for all paginators

This shared base class is used by DateTimePaginator, which the audit log endpoint uses on every default request, so the change alters behavior well beyond the opt-in path. A forged next cursor with a negative offset is now silently served from the start of the result set instead of failing, while a forged prev cursor with a negative offset still raises from Django slicing. Invalid input is now accepted inconsistently. The inline comment that this is 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is wrong: the queryset rejects negative slices, and the clamp is what changes the outcome. The existing code validates offsets elsewhere (for example the `if self.offset < 0` checks in other paginators), so this should be an explicit validation or be reverted.

Comment claims permissions are enforced at the queryset level, which this branch does not do

The comment says 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Nothing in this branch checks permissions. The endpoint's permission class has already run, and the queryset is only filtered by organization_id. The comment justifies a deliberately wider access path, which would mislead future maintainers into treating unchecked negative-offset access as vetted. The claim should be removed, and the branch should be removed unless a real use case is demonstrated.

The 'optimized' path issues the same query as the default path, so it gives no performance benefit

The opted-in branch uses the same queryset, ordering, and slicing as DateTimePaginator. The only differences are the broken get_item_key and the unreachable negative-offset branch. The PR title and comments claim high-performance, efficient traversal, but no query, index, or benchmark change supports that. The PR description is just 'Test 1', so there is no stated rationale or measurement. The comments and title should not claim a performance gain unless one is demonstrated.

Comment says negative cursor offsets are supported, but nothing validates or handles them

The added comments state that negative offsets are allowed and 'enable efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions'. The change here is only a comment, and Cursor accepts whatever int() returns, including values parsed from untrusted request input via from_string. The paginators either raise on negative slices or silently clamp them, so the comment describes behavior that does not exist and documents an input the server never validates. Remove the comment or add real validation.

New paginator, new query parameter, and changed base behavior have no tests

The PR adds a public experimental query parameter (optimized_pagination), a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class with its own get_result and get_item_key, and changes BasePaginator.get_result, which every DateTimePaginator caller relies on. No tests are added or updated. A single request from an admin with at least one audit log row would have exposed the TypeError in get_item_key. Tests should cover: the opted-in admin path with rows, the non-admin fallback to DateTimePaginator, the member-less caller case, and how negative cursor offsets are handled on both the next and prev paths.
